pharm: Cardiac glycoside that inhibits the sodium-potassium ATPase pump, increasing myocardial contractility and vagal tone; has a narrow therapeutic index.
quick: Consistent timing; high-fiber meals reduce absorption
Used when indicated; monitor levels (volume changes)
Reduce dose - renally eliminated; key toxicity factor
Serum digoxin level, potassium, magnesium, renal function, ECG
summary: Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside used for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and for ventricular rate control in atrial fibrillation. It has a narrow therapeutic index - toxic levels are only slightly above therapeutic - so dosing is individualized by lean body weight, age, and renal function, with serum level and electrolyte monitoring. Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, and renal impairment increase toxicity risk. It is contraindicated in ventricular fibrillation.
indications: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (to improve symptoms; usually added to standard therapy)
Control of ventricular response rate in chronic atrial fibrillation

dosage.t: Give half initially, then 1/4 every 6-8 h x2 with reassessment
dosage.n: Optional; reassess clinical response and toxicity before each dose
Adjust per lean body weight, renal function, age, levels; increase no more often than every 2 weeks
Use oral solution for accurate dosing in small patients
Digoxin is largely renally eliminated; major toxicity factor

admin: Individualize dose by lean body weight, age, renal function, and concomitant drugs
Use oral solution for infants, young children, or very low body weight for accuracy
Maintain consistent timing relative to meals; high-fiber/bran meals reduce absorption
Reduce dose in renal impairment and reassess after starting interacting drugs
Consider interrupting/reducing dose before electrical cardioversion
moa: Inhibits the myocardial sodium-potassium ATPase, raising intracellular sodium and (via sodium-calcium exchange) intracellular calcium, increasing the force of contraction (positive inotropy). It also increases vagal (parasympathetic) tone, slowing AV-nodal conduction and ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to digoxin or other digitalis preparations
relative: Sick sinus syndrome or AV block without pacemaker

preg: Used when clinically indicated (e.g., maternal or fetal arrhythmia); pregnancy alters pharmacokinetics so monitor serum levels and adjust dose. Crosses the placenta.
lact: Excreted in breast milk in small amounts; considered compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: Digoxin is primarily eliminated renally; reduce dose and lengthen interval in renal impairment. Declining renal function is a leading cause of toxicity - reassess dose accordingly.
hepatic: No major dosage adjustment required (predominantly renal elimination).

major: P-glycoprotein inhibitors (amiodarone, quinidine, verapamil, dronedarone, clarithromycin, itraconazole, cyclosporine, ritonavir) - raise digoxin levels; reduce digoxin dose
Drugs causing hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia (loop/thiazide diuretics, amphotericin B) - increase toxicity risk
Calcium (especially rapid IV) - precipitates arrhythmia in digitalized patients
moderate: Beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine CCBs - additive AV-nodal slowing/bradycardia
Spironolactone - may raise levels and interfere with some assays
Antacids, kaolin-pectin, cholestyramine, high-fiber meals - reduce absorption
minor: St. John's wort (P-gp induction) - may lower levels
interactions.food: High-fiber/bran meals reduce absorption; take consistently relative to food.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor serum digoxin level (target ~0.5-0.9 ng/mL in heart failure; sample >=6-8 h post-dose), potassium, magnesium, calcium, and renal function; certain drugs (spironolactone) can interfere with immunoassays.

serious: Cardiac arrhythmias (PVCs, bigeminy, AV block, atrial tachycardia with block, ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation)

monitoring: Serum digoxin concentration (sample at least 6-8 hours after a dose)
Signs/symptoms of toxicity (GI upset, visual changes, arrhythmia, confusion)
counsel: Take at the same time each day exactly as prescribed; do not skip or double doses
Report nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, blurred or yellow-tinged vision, palpitations, or feeling faint - these can be signs of toxicity
Have regular blood tests for digoxin level, potassium, and kidney function
Tell your clinician before starting any new medicine, including over-the-counter and herbal products
Maintain a consistent diet; avoid sudden large changes in potassium intake
pk: Store at room temperature, protect from light
pearls: Narrow therapeutic index - toxic levels are only slightly above therapeutic; individualize and monitor levels
Lower target level (~0.5-0.9 ng/mL) is associated with better outcomes in heart failure
Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypercalcemia markedly increase toxicity risk
Renal impairment is a leading cause of accumulation and toxicity - reduce dose
Many drugs raise levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition (amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine) - reduce digoxin dose
Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab) reverse life-threatening toxicity
missed: If a dose is missed and it is within about 12 hours, take it; if more than 12 hours have passed, skip it and take the next dose at the usual time. Never double the dose. If two or more days of doses are missed, contact the prescriber.
overdose: Toxicity causes GI symptoms, visual disturbances, confusion, and dangerous arrhythmias; acute overdose typically causes hyperkalemia. Management: discontinue digoxin, correct electrolytes (treat hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia; in acute toxicity manage hyperkalemia cautiously - avoid IV calcium), monitor ECG, treat bradyarrhythmias with atropine/pacing, and give digoxin immune Fab (DigiFab) for life-threatening arrhythmias, hemodynamic instability, or marked hyperkalemia. Dialysis is ineffective (large volume of distribution).
